text:
I think 1440p / 144hz+ makes the most sense for ALL the 4000 series GPU's generally speaking - Sure the RTX 4090 (same is true of the RTX 4080 in many cases as well) can run many games at 4K@ 100FPS+ but there are still plenty of cases where 1440p makes more sense if you want to play at max settings w/ ray tracing, etc. & 120fps+ It would appear the "optimal" use case scenario for the RTX 4090 is to have both a 4K/120hz+ display and a 1440p/144hz+ display depending on the game..  If I had to pick (1) I'd still go with a high refresh 1440p display. 

As far as the RTX 4070Ti sure it makes the most sense from purely a cost to performance matrix and will run current AAA games at 1440p/ 120fps+ no problem but going forward the 12GB of VRAM may present an issue / limitations' in the years to come. Don't hear me wrong I still think this is a pretty damn good card regardless considering the market conditions. 

The RTX 4080 makes the most sense to me as 1440p / 144hz+ gaming is still the "sweet spot" IMO and with 16GB of VRAM it is likely to hold up better than the 4070TI for high refresh 1440p gaming with plenty of "headroom" during the most graphically demanding moments. Sure, even the RTX 4080 may seem a bit "overkill" for 1440p (game dependent of course) but remember games are only going to become more demanding going forward. 

I'm personally waiting to see benchmarks on the AMD Ryzen 9 7000 series "X3D" cards and likely to pair the Ryzen 9 7900X3D (granted it's performance justifies the cost over the 7900X) with RTX 4080 and plan to run this setup for ~ 5 years. I have both an OLED 4K/ 120hz display via HDMI 2.1 (LG B9 55' inch) and (2) - 27" 1440p/ 165hz - ViewSonic XG27OQG monitors but will likely game solely on my 27" ViewSonic monitor - This is a phenomenal gaming monitor BTW (27"  1440p - IPS Nano Color - G-SYNC - 1ms (GtG) - 165hz OC - 98% DCI-P3 - etc.)  albeit a bit pricy at ~ $700.00. 

When it comes to the RTX "3000" series cards it's also important to consider the "power requirements" as the new 4000 series are generally much more efficient in this regard (will be reflected in your power bill.) and the updated feature sets will provide more advantages down the road as well. It's like when you're purchasing a vehicle for example, the MSRP is NOT the "only" factor to consider as the "running cost / feature set" are a huge factor in the overall equation when it comes to the value proposition.

Mem bandwidth simply can not be the cause of hitches in games - it does not work that way. You can easily check if that is true by lowering your card memory frequency (for example, via Afterburner) - you will see that the lower the memory frequency (and thus the lower the bandwidth) is, the lower framerate you get in terms of both average and 1% lows. And there is linear relationship between average and 1% lows in this case.
I tried to overclock VRAM and got ~20% higher bandwidth (about 600 GB/s), but it does not make any big difference at 1440p anyway (~5%). Ti Super will have 672 GB/s bandwidth, which is 33% more than what Ti offers. This means that this additional bandwidth will provide ~10% more frames vs stock Ti, at best.

text:
@pietervandermeersch9667  I'm not sure how they implement it in UE5 to be honest. I can only make assumptions. But my guess was that they started developing their solution before hardware accelerated ray tracing got implemented across vendors.

Because it doesn't matter as much for companies like Epic whether Nvidia brings such a feature to the table as long as other vendors do not follow. Their game engine aims to be used for many AAA console titles. So since current consoles only provide RDNA2, it's not really feasible to push heavy effects using the hardware acceleration path. You just loose more control when it comes to optimization using a fixed hardware path.

That's why many game companies still do not even bother with ray tracing effects. It's not even usable for most consumers and the ones benefiting most from the features existence work in content creation to be honest.

So until game consoles bring full path tracing capabilities, I don't think any game will require it. So there's still more need to optimize rasterization pipelines.

Honestly the most interesting aspects I see in ray tracing besides reflections should be transparencies. Because that's something rasterization completely lacks. Sure, you can render transparent objects as last step in pipeline but ordering them correctly is close to impossible and blending them properly a nightmare. ^^'
author: @thejackimonster9689

text:
@SKHYJINXBenchmarks  I think their software solution lacks certain features. Also I don't think it's the HW RT which is slower but their whole DX12 render pipeline in comparison to the DX11 pipeline. That shouldn't be a surprise since DX11 is much older than DX12 and the API is much more low level.

So development of DX12 should be overall slower in many cases, explaining the issues many games still have with it.

Usually the hardware accelerated ray tracing should beat any comparable software solution in performance. Because having a fixed function hardware reduces the latency of processing code.

For example on Linux you get with RADV (a Vulkan driver) a software pipeline for ray tracing. So you can use ray tracing pipelines and new features without the actual hardware acceleration support for them. But the software solution runs at about half the speed depending on the test case.
